units.title: Discovering Sub-atomic Particles
units.short_description: Follow the experiments that revealed electrons, protons, and neutrons, and connect each particle with its charge and mass.

ncert_sections.title: Charge to Mass Ratio of Electron

concepts.title: Atoms as Collections of Sub-atomic Particles
Cathode Rays and the Discovery of the Electron
Thomson's Electron Charge-to-Mass Experiment
Millikan's Measurement of Electron Charge
Canal Rays, Protons, and Neutrons
Charge and Mass of Electron, Proton, and Neutron

skills: Interpret cathode-ray and canal-ray observations as evidence for sub-atomic particles.
Relate electron deflection to the charge-to-mass ratio measured by Thomson.
Explain how Millikan's oil-drop experiment established the electron's charge.
Compare the relative charge and approximate mass of electrons, protons, and neutrons.
units.why_it_matters: The experiments in this unit replace the idea of an indivisible atom with evidence-based particles and measurements used by every later atomic model.
learning_route: Read each discharge-tube observation and identify what it proves.
Connect Thomson's and Millikan's measurements to electron mass and charge.
Compare electrons, protons, and neutrons using NCERT Table 2.1.
Finish with a short evidence-to-conclusion check.
mastery_criteria: Explain why cathode-ray behaviour supports electrons being present in every atom.
Distinguish what Thomson measured from what Millikan measured.
Use charge and mass data to compare all three fundamental particles.
Solve a short particle-count or total-charge problem with correct units.

units.title: Atomic Models and Nuclear Identity
units.short_description: Compare Thomson and Rutherford models, interpret the scattering experiment, and use atomic and mass numbers to identify atoms, isotopes, and isobars.

source_segments.end_anchor: 2.3 Developments Leading to the Bohr's Model of Atom

concepts.title: Why Atomic Models Are Needed
Thomson's Uniform Positive Sphere Model
Rutherford's Alpha-particle Scattering Experiment

Isotopes, Isobars, and Nuclide Notation
Atomic Stability and Other Limits of Rutherford's Model

skills: Predict Rutherford-scattering observations from Thomson's model and compare them with the actual results.
Infer the size, charge, and location of the nucleus from alpha-particle deflections.
Calculate numbers of protons, neutrons, and electrons from atomic notation or ionic charge.
Distinguish isotopes from isobars and explain why isotopes have similar chemical behaviour.
Explain why Rutherford's orbiting-electron model cannot account for atomic stability.
units.why_it_matters: This unit turns experimental observations into a model of the nucleus and gives the notation needed to describe every atomic species accurately.
learning_route: Compare what Thomson's model predicts with Rutherford's observations.
Build Rutherford's nuclear model from the three scattering conclusions.
Use Z, A, and ionic charge to count particles and classify nuclides.
Identify the stability problem that the next model must solve.
mastery_criteria: Derive Rutherford's three conclusions from the scattering observations rather than recalling them without evidence.
Correctly determine protons, neutrons, and electrons for neutral atoms and ions.
Classify and represent unfamiliar isotope and isobar examples using nuclide notation.
Explain at least two limitations of Rutherford's model, including the atomic-stability problem.

units.title: Radiation, Quanta, and Atomic Spectra
units.short_description: Connect wave properties, Planck's quantum idea, the photoelectric effect, and hydrogen line spectra to the evidence that atomic energies are quantized.

Evidence for the Quantized Electronic Energy Levels: Atomic Spectra

skills: Relate wavelength, frequency, wavenumber, and the speed of electromagnetic radiation.
Locate a radiation within the electromagnetic spectrum from its wavelength or frequency.
Calculate photon energy and molar photon energy using Planck's relation.
Use threshold frequency and work function to reason about the photoelectric effect.
Distinguish continuous, emission-line, and absorption spectra.
Use the Balmer or Rydberg relation to interpret hydrogen spectral lines.
units.why_it_matters: Bohr's model only makes sense after the student sees the experimental evidence that radiation and atomic energy exchange occur in discrete quantities.
learning_route: Build the wavelength-frequency-wavenumber relationship and map the spectrum.
Use black-body and photoelectric observations to understand Planck's quantum idea.
Compare continuous and atomic line spectra.
Read the hydrogen series as evidence for discrete electronic energies.
mastery_criteria: Convert accurately among wavelength, frequency, and wavenumber with correct units.
Calculate photon energy and explain why intensity and frequency play different roles in the photoelectric effect.
Distinguish continuous, emission, and absorption spectra from descriptions or diagrams.
Identify the hydrogen spectral series and use a supplied relation to calculate or explain a transition.

units.title: Bohr's Hydrogen Atom
units.short_description: Use Bohr's postulates to connect allowed orbits, quantized energies, electronic transitions, and the hydrogen spectrum, then recognise where the model fails.

ncert_sections.title: Explanation of Line Spectrum of Hydrogen

source_segments.end_anchor: 2.5 Towards Quantum Mechanical Model of the Atom

Limitations of Bohr's Model

skills: State and interpret Bohr's postulates rather than treating them as isolated facts.
Calculate orbit radius and energy for hydrogen and hydrogen-like species.
Determine whether a transition represents absorption or emission and calculate its energy, frequency, or wavelength.
Connect a hydrogen transition with the appropriate spectral series.
Explain the successes and limitations of Bohr's model.
units.why_it_matters: Bohr's model is the first chapter model that quantitatively connects atomic structure with energy and spectra, while its limitations motivate quantum mechanics.
learning_route: Translate each Bohr postulate into a picture of allowed states and transitions.
Use the radius and energy relations for hydrogen-like species.
Calculate absorption or emission quantities and connect them to spectral lines.
Finish by identifying precisely what the model still cannot explain.
mastery_criteria: Explain the meaning of stationary states and quantized angular momentum.
Use Bohr relations accurately for H, He+, or another one-electron species.
Solve a transition problem with correct sign, energy, frequency, wavelength, and spectral-series interpretation.
State at least two model limitations and explain why they matter.

units.title: From Orbits to Quantum Mechanics
units.short_description: Use de Broglie's matter waves and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle to understand why exact electron paths must give way to a probability-based model.

ncert_sections.title: Towards Quantum Mechanical Model of the Atom

source_segments.start_anchor: 2.5 Towards Quantum Mechanical Model of the Atom

concepts.title: Why Atomic Theory Must Move Beyond Bohr Orbits
Wave-particle Duality of Matter
de Broglie Wavelength and Particle Momentum
Heisenberg's Position-Momentum Uncertainty Principle
Why Uncertainty Matters for Electrons but Not Everyday Objects

skills: Calculate de Broglie wavelength from mass and velocity or momentum.
Compare why wave behaviour is observable for microscopic particles but negligible for macroscopic objects.
Apply the uncertainty relation to position, velocity, or momentum estimates.
Explain why the idea of a precise electron trajectory conflicts with quantum evidence.
units.why_it_matters: These two principles explain why electrons cannot be treated as tiny planets and establish the conceptual foundation for atomic orbitals.
learning_route: Connect matter-wave behaviour with de Broglie's wavelength relation.
Compare electron and everyday-object wavelengths through short calculations.
Use the uncertainty principle to test what can be known simultaneously.
Replace the idea of an exact orbit with a probability-based description.
mastery_criteria: Calculate and compare de Broglie wavelengths with correct SI units.
Use Heisenberg's relation to find an uncertainty and interpret its physical meaning.
Explain why quantum effects are consequential for electrons but usually negligible for macroscopic objects.
Justify why an atomic orbital is not the same as a Bohr orbit.

units.title: Quantum Numbers and Atomic Orbitals
units.short_description: Build the probability model of the atom, use four quantum numbers to describe electrons, and interpret orbital shapes, orientations, and nodes.

concepts.title: Quantum Mechanical Model and the Schrodinger Equation
Wave Function, Atomic Orbital, and Probability Density

Boundary Surfaces and Shapes of s, p, and d Orbitals

skills: Distinguish an orbital probability distribution from a fixed electron path.
Determine allowed n, l, ml, and ms values and reject impossible combinations.
Calculate the number of subshells, orbitals, and possible electrons for a shell or subshell.
Identify s, p, and d orbital shapes and orientations from diagrams.
Calculate radial, angular, and total nodes for an orbital.
units.why_it_matters: Quantum numbers and orbitals provide the language for locating electron probability, counting available states, and building electronic configurations correctly.
learning_route: Move from the Schrodinger model to wave functions, orbitals, and probability density.
Build the allowed values and meaning of all four quantum numbers.
Connect quantum numbers to shell, subshell, orientation, and electron capacity.
Read orbital-shape diagrams and calculate their nodes.
mastery_criteria: Explain the physical meaning of probability density and why a wave function defines an orbital.
Validate or construct complete quantum-number sets without violating allowed ranges.
Determine shell and subshell capacities from quantum numbers.
Identify s, p, and d orbitals and correctly calculate radial, angular, and total nodes.

units.title: Orbital Energies and Electronic Configuration
units.short_description: Order orbitals, apply Aufbau, Pauli, and Hund rules, write electronic configurations, and explain the stability of half-filled and fully filled subshells.

skills: Compare orbital energy order in hydrogen and multi-electron atoms.
Apply the n + l rule and shielding ideas to compare orbital energies.
Use Aufbau, Pauli, and Hund rules together to fill orbital diagrams.
Write full and noble-gas electronic configurations for atoms and ions.
Identify valence electrons and unpaired electrons.
Explain chromium and copper exceptions using half-filled and fully filled subshell stability.
units.why_it_matters: Electronic configuration is the chapter's practical outcome and becomes the foundation for periodicity, bonding, reactivity, and later chemistry.
learning_route: Order orbitals using hydrogen degeneracy, shielding, and the n + l rule.
Apply Aufbau, Pauli, and Hund rules to orbital diagrams.
Write full and noble-gas configurations and identify valence electrons.
Explain stable half-filled and fully filled patterns, including Cr and Cu.
mastery_criteria: Correctly compare energies of orbitals in hydrogen and multi-electron atoms.
Construct orbital diagrams without violating Aufbau, Pauli, or Hund rules.
Write accurate electronic configurations for unfamiliar atoms and common ions and identify unpaired electrons.
Explain Cr and Cu exceptions using symmetry and exchange-energy ideas from NCERT.
